notes.1a: Large majority of the candidate responses correctly identified the region of the world with the highest number of internet users as Asia from Source 1, and, therefore, achieved the one mark.
notes.1b: Majority of the candidate responses identified two benefits of the internet for young people from Source 2, and, therefore, achieved the maximum of two marks.
notes.1c: Most of the candidates responded very well to this question, identifying and justifying a benefit of the internet for young people which, in their opinion, was the most important. Most of the candidate responses discussed providing information, communicating with others and to develop employability. 0457 Global Perspectives November 2020 The most common justifications given related to the issues of impact included: • the number of people affected; • impact on individual or group life chances, lifestyle and employment; • the long-term positive implications and consequences; • impact on other aspects of social, political and economic life. Many of the candidate responses showed awareness of the link between cause and consequence in this context, as well as the ‘virtuous circle’ effect of a consequence or cause leading to another. The most successful responses gave several clear reasons to explain why one benefit was more important than others. The less successful responses often simply stated the benefit without explanation and relied on assertion without evidence or careful reasoning. Some of the candidate responses compared the significance of different benefits, but this was not necessary to achieve full marks.
notes.1d: Many of the candidates responded well to this question and explained why the use of the internet by young people is important for governments. These responses demonstrated a clear understanding of the concept of ‘national’ and government perspectives. Candidate responses achieving higher marks provided a clearly reasoned, credible and structured explanation. There were many thoughtful discussions of the impact of the internet on young people and the government of countries, including education, the social life of local communities and wider economic growth, as well as cultural issues. Some of the candidate responses introduced issues of cooperation between countries and governments through cultural and technological exchange. The less successful responses often gave a weak explanation or asserted opinion about the internet in general without reference to the national dimension of the question. Some of the candidate responses simply listed a range of consequences of the internet taken directly from the sources without any explanation or linking to the ‘national’ context.
notes.2a: Most of the candidate responses evaluated the argument in Source 3 and assess how well the author supported the view that ‘we are spending too much on computers’. The most often identified strengths of the argument were: • some evidence about the personal experience of daughter and a local business; • strong tone of language – passionate; • uses an expert as evidence – a professor; • range of evidence. The most often identified weaknesses of the argument were: • few facts and statistics to back up claim; • sources not clearly referenced; • potential newspaper bias; • author unknown – difficult to verify knowledge claims and authenticity; • emotive tone of language. The most successful responses provided clearly reasoned, credible and structured explanation for their opinions, usually discussing four or more distinct evaluative points. The less successful responses often simply stated or asserted an opinion. Some of the less successful responses described the reasons and evidence within the source but did not evaluate or explain why the identified reason or type of evidence was a strength or a weakness. Candidates should be encouraged to give a clear and explicit statement about the quality of the reasons and evidence in the source, and justify their opinion using the material in the source as evidence. This includes quoting from or summarising elements of the source.
notes.2b: The more successful candidate responses described several methods, sources of information and types of evidence that could be used to test the claim that ‘the costs of technology are increasing every year’. The methods of testing the claim suggested were carefully explained and clearly related to the claim. Candidate responses often described interviews, surveys and questionnaires with people about the issue, for example, from the public, manufacturers and sellers of technology. Surveys of local shops were also suggested. Other methods included consultation with experts, local government and consumer researchers. Large majority of the candidate responses suggested secondary research using sources from the internet. Many described the type of source that was likely to be reliable and free from bias or vested interest, for example, from governments, NGOs and United Nations organisations. The most successful responses provided clearly reasoned, credible and structured explanation for their suggestions clearly and explicitly linked to the claim being tested. The less successful responses often simply stated or listed several methods or sources of evidence but did not explain them fully or make the link between the evidence being gathered and how it could be used to evaluate the claim being tested. A few candidate responses described their opinion on the issue rather than describing how it could be researched. This did not answer the question. Candidates should be encouraged to regularly practice designing research strategies to test claims or answer research questions as a part of their course.
notes.3a: A large majority of the candidate responses correctly identified a prediction from Kim’s statement and explained that predictions are statements or claims about events in the future. Most of the candidate responses justified and explained their judgement well.
notes.3b: Most of the candidate responses correctly identified a fact from Sumin’s statement and explained that facts are statements that are true or correct and can be verified. Most of the candidate responses justified and explained their judgement well.
notes.3c: Many of the candidate responses correctly identified an example of a vested interest in Sumin’s statement, showing an understanding that a vested interest is a strong view about something because you could get a personal of financial advantage from the situation. Candidate responses most frequently identified the following examples of vested interest from the Sumin’s statement: • as an author she wanted to sell more of her books; • she emphasised the dangers of the internet to persuade parents to buy her publications; • she was pleased to speak on a local radio programme to bring attention to her work. The most successful responses often quoted from the source and clearly described evidence taken from the source to support their judgment. This question was challenging for some, as some candidate responses did not show an understanding of the concept of vested interest and did not use the idea in the analysis of source material. Centres should encourage candidates to develop their understanding of the term ‘vested interest’ and provide experience of using the term in the analysis of sources, alongside other critical thinking concepts like value judgement, bias, fact, opinion and prediction.
notes.3d: Large majority of the candidate responses compared both statements explicitly (Kim’s and Sumins), and discussed issues relating to evidence, language, knowledge claims and expertise. Some of the candidate responses also addressed the reasons and values within each statement. 0457 Global Perspectives November 2020 The most successful responses presented well supported judgements about the arguments with a clear assessment of the value of each statement. This included coherent, structured evaluation of how well the argument worked with a focus on reasons and evidence, with a range of points about knowledge claims, consequences and values for both statements. These responses were usually balanced with a clear conclusion. The statements were also quoted explicitly and material from the statements was used directly in the response as evidence to support candidate’s opinion. In the less successful responses, the discussion lacked support and tended to be mainly asserted with little clarity of argument. These responses often focused on issues rather than reasons, knowledge claims, evidence, consequences or values. There was also very little or no overt evaluation seen. Centres should encourage candidates to frequently practice comparing and evaluating sources. This should involve a consideration of the reasons and evidence used to support the argument or perspective in the source.
notes.4: In this question, candidates were asked to evaluate the argument that young people need to be protected from the internet because it is harmful. Candidates were asked to justify their views using material drawn from the sources as well as their own experience and evidence. There were many thoughtful discussions of the view seen. However, some of the candidate responses often described their opinions in a generalised and asserted way. Most of the candidate responses suggested that protection from the internet was not justified due to the potential benefits for young people that outweighed the dangers. The most successful responses often were well supported, gave logical reasoning and made clear judgements about the issue. A clear, balanced assessment or conclusion was also seen, as these responses linked the argument back to the issue. Responses that achieved lower marks were often generalised, lacked relevance to the issue and simply described their own opinion about the internet. Arguments were often unsupported and asserted. To help candidates prepare for successfully answering this type of question, centres should encourage candidates to regularly practice writing extended essays in which they contrast and compare different perspectives or potential actions in response to an issue. This would help candidates to analyse and evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of the reasons and evidence that supports and justifies the perspective or action.
notes.key_messages:
• Candidate responses demonstrated very good skills of interpretation and analysis.
• Evaluation was done with more confidence.
• Candidates should be encouraged to explain research designs fully.
• Candidates should be encouraged to use material from sources as evidence to justify their opinions.
notes.general_comments:
This question paper consists of compulsory questions based on a range of sources, which present global
issues from different perspectives. This question paper was based on source material related to the topic of
Globalisation and explored the role of the internet in globalisation and education.
Overall, the standard of candidate responses was good. Many of the candidate responses clearly identified
the different perspectives on global issues and used credible arguments to support their own points of view.
Candidate responses also interpreted and analysed the sources and data presented in different ways.
However, candidates should be encouraged to carefully explain research designs and choice of research
methods in greater detail, explicitly when relating their research strategy to the claim being tested. Good
evaluation skills were seen, and many candidate responses identified and explained a range of strengths
and weaknesses in evidence and argument.
Candidate responses explored different perspectives on the issues related to globalisation and the internet
raised within the sources. Both arguments and counterarguments for different perspectives were explored in
the consideration of global issues. However, candidates should be encouraged to practise the skills of
presenting reasons and evidence to justify an opinion, perspective or proposal. Role play, drama,
presentation and debate, in which candidates present different perspectives on an issue, could help to
develop these skills further.
